02 / The problem

Small drones are found by radar. The usual fix costs more than the drone can carry.

1

Radar is how small drones get found

Counter-drone radar is now the main way small uncrewed aircraft are detected. An aircraft that is seen sooner is stopped sooner.

2

Today's fix is added on afterward

Radar-absorbing coatings and add-on materials bring weight, cost and hand labor. They do not hold up well on aircraft built to be low cost and expendable.

3

The alternative has never been measured

DARC is a molded structural material with electrical properties that may affect radar return. If the structure did part of the job, it would come with the airframe, with no added step.

Problem
statement

BGS and DFA cannot tell whether DARC reduces the radar signature of a small aircraft, or by how much. Neither company has the radar range, instruments or expertise to find out, and neither can responsibly invest in an airframe until it knows.

03 / Who we are: BGS Engineering

BGS: three friends, a car part, and the Albuquerque sun

We set out to mold a carbon fiber car part that would not break down in New Mexico sunlight. The material we ended up with does more than we asked of it.

Matt Gassner, Jerry Stratton and Dan Brockett have been friends for 25 years. Jerry is a mold maker, Dan runs operations and logistics, and Matt came from finance. None of us is a materials scientist, so we took our questions to NMSBA and Sandia.

The result is DARC, Discontinuous Advanced Resin Composite: a carbon fiber composite that is pressed in a mold to its finished shape, with no autoclave. BGS makes and sells finished molded parts. We do not sell raw material.

The composition is patent pending and the molding process is proprietary. Tooling, molding and inspection happen in our own building in Albuquerque.

What we know about DARC today

Confirmed

A structural carbon fiber composite, molded to shape in one step.

Confirmed

It conducts electricity and blocks radio energy, with nothing added on.

By design, not yet tested

UV durability. It was the design goal. Weathering tests are still ahead.

Under investigation

Radar signature. That is the question in this proposal.

06 / Why it is worth measuring

Three reasons DARC might return less radar energy. None is proven yet.

1A softer boundary than metal

Metal is a mirror to radar. DARC is only partly conductive, so some of the wave may enter the material instead of bouncing off its face.

2Energy lost as heat

Inside a partial conductor the wave drives small currents that fade away as heat, leaving less to come back out.

3Scattering by random fibers

Short fibers point in every direction. They may break up what remains and send it many ways instead of straight back.

Confirmed

DARC conducts electricity. In independent low-frequency tests it blocked radio energy. Those tests did not measure radar return.

Supported by physics

All three effects are established for this class of material. None has been confirmed on DARC.

Under investigation

How much energy comes back to a radar, at the frequencies that matter, compared with what small drones are built from today.

07 / Why a measured number matters

A guess is not good enough. The payoff depends on the size of the number.

If the radar return drops by

3 dB
84%

of the original detection range

71% of the area covered

Return cut byIn plain termsDetection rangeArea covered
3 dBHalf84%71%
6 dBOne quarter71%50%
10 dBOne tenth56%32%
20 dBOne hundredth32%10%

Detection range shrinks slowly as radar return falls. Halving the return only trims range to 84%. Cutting it to a tenth roughly halves the range. A small effect buys little. A large one changes the mission.

Where DARC falls on this scale is unknown. Material is also only part of the picture: motors, battery, wiring and shape all reflect. That is why the project has two parts.

Radar-equation physics, the same for any material. The steps are a what-if scale. They are not a DARC measurement or an expected result.

08 / What the aircraft still has to do

The answer has to work on a real aircraft, not just a test plate

Radios have to see outGPS and data links need clear paths through the structure. Absorbing everywhere is not an option.
Sensors need openingsCameras and other sensors need apertures in the shell.
Heat has to leaveOnboard computing and power electronics must stay cool.
Everything has to fitPayload, battery and flight computer set the shape as much as radar does.
Every gram countsAt this size the structure has to be thin-walled and light.
It has to be moldableDraft angles, even wall thickness, no deep undercuts.
It has to flyStable at low speed, launched and recovered in the field.
No added stepsThe benefit has to come from the molded part itself, with no coating afterward.

Radar bands of most interest to DFA: X band and Ku band, where small-drone detection radars commonly operate.

09 / What we are asking the lab to help answer

Two questions, in order, with a stop between them

Question 1: measure

Does DARC send less radar energy back than the materials small drones are built from today?

Flat DARC samples, compared against benchmark materials, across thickness, angle and frequency.

Question 2: design

If so, how should an airframe be shaped and laid out to use it?

Measured properties go into radar modeling of a representative airframe that still has to carry radios, sensors and payload, and still has to be moldable.

Stop

Both companies drop the idea and spend nothing more on it. A clear no is a useful result.

Why a national lab

This takes a radar range, calibrated instruments and modeling tools working together. Neither company has them, and buying them piecemeal from several vendors is beyond a small business.

What we bring

BGS supplies DARC samples, molding knowledge and design-for-manufacture input. DFA supplies the aircraft requirements, layout constraints and a platform to design around.

Sandia's role, scope and deliverables will be set by the Sandia principal investigator once confirmed. This slide describes the companies' request only.

11 / Cost reduction

One benefit does not wait on radar: 45 parts become 2

45

parts in the MkIV frame

13 plates + 32 fasteners

A conventional small-drone frame is flat plates cut and bolted together. Every part has to be bought, stocked, assembled and inspected.

A molded airframe is two shell halves bonded together. Fewer parts means fewer suppliers, less assembly labor and fewer fasteners to work loose.

This holds whatever the radar measurement shows. It is the cost-reduction case for molding the airframe in the first place.

Layout is schematic. Part counts are actual. No dollar savings are claimed yet.
